Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
Personal financial literacy should be a required subject in secondary schools because its absence has been shown to correlate with high rates of consumer debt and financial vulnerability among young adults. Many young people enter adulthood without a basic understanding of budgeting, saving, or managing credit, leaving them susceptible to poor financial decisions. This lack of knowledge often leads to accumulating debt, struggling with loan repayments, and facing long-term financial instability. By equipping students with financial literacy before they encounter these challenges, schools can help mitigate the risks associated with financial illiteracy and foster a generation of informed, responsible consumers. Financial literacy is a universal life skill that benefits all students, regardless of their income or career path. Whether pursuing higher education, entering the workforce, or starting a business, every individual will encounter financial decisions that impact their livelihood. Understanding concepts like interest rates, taxes, investments, and retirement planning is essential for navigating adulthood successfully. Moreover, financial literacy empowers students from diverse backgrounds to break cycles of poverty, make informed choices, and achieve financial independence. By teaching these skills, schools can level the playing field and ensure that all students have the tools they need to thrive in a complex economic landscape. Schools are uniquely positioned to provide this education because they are the only institution with reliable access to all young people before they face high-stakes financial decisions. Unlike other organizations or community programs, schools reach nearly every student, regardless of socioeconomic status or geographic location. This universal access ensures that financial literacy education is not limited to those who actively seek it out or can afford specialized courses. By integrating financial literacy into the secondary school curriculum, educators can proactively prepare students for the financial realities they will encounter as adults, reducing the likelihood of costly mistakes and fostering long-term financial well-being.

--- RESPONSE B ---
Personal financial literacy should be a required subject in secondary schools because the absence of financial education is closely linked to high rates of consumer debt and financial vulnerability among young adults. Many students leave school expected to manage bank accounts, credit cards, student loans, rent, taxes, insurance, and digital payment systems without having been taught how interest, budgeting, borrowing, or risk work. When young adults do not understand compound interest, minimum payments, credit scores, or the long-term cost of debt, they are more likely to make decisions that leave them financially strained for years. Required financial education would give students practical knowledge before they encounter these pressures, helping them recognize harmful borrowing patterns, plan for expenses, and avoid preventable financial instability.

Financial literacy is also a universal life skill that benefits all students, regardless of income, academic goals, or career path. Every student will eventually need to earn, spend, save, borrow, file taxes, compare costs, evaluate contracts, and make choices about housing, transportation, healthcare, education, and retirement. These skills are not limited to students entering business, finance, or college; they are necessary for anyone who will participate in the economy as a worker, consumer, renter, homeowner, parent, or citizen. Making financial literacy required ensures that all students receive a common foundation for making informed decisions in everyday life.

Schools are the only institution with reliable access to nearly all young people before they face high-stakes financial decisions. Families vary widely in their ability, time, and confidence to teach financial concepts, and not all students have access to trusted guidance outside the classroom. By the time many young adults seek information on their own, they may already be signing loan agreements, opening credit accounts, choosing employment benefits, or committing to major expenses. Secondary schools are uniquely positioned to provide consistent instruction before those decisions arrive, making financial literacy a necessary part of preparing students for adulthood.

--- RESPONSE C ---
Personal financial literacy belongs in the required curriculum of every secondary school, and the evidence supporting this claim grows more compelling with each passing year. Young adults in their twenties increasingly find themselves ensnared in patterns of debt and financial precariousness that shadow them for decades, and the connection between this vulnerability and the absence of formal financial education is difficult to ignore. Credit card balances among Americans under thirty routinely climb into the thousands, student loan borrowers frequently sign promissory notes without grasping amortization or the long-term weight of accrued interest, and surveys consistently reveal that a majority of young adults cannot cover an unexpected expense of a few hundred dollars without borrowing. These are not failures of character but failures of preparation. When young people enter adulthood never having been taught how compound interest multiplies debt, how credit scores shape access to housing and employment, or how to construct even a rudimentary budget, the predictable outcome is widespread financial fragility. The correlation between absent instruction and poor outcomes is not incidental; it reflects a straightforward truth that people cannot apply knowledge they have never been given.

The value of this knowledge, moreover, extends to every student regardless of family wealth, academic trajectory, or intended profession. Unlike subjects whose relevance depends on specialization, financial literacy addresses decisions that every adult without exception must make. The young person who enters a trade must understand paychecks, taxes, and retirement contributions just as surely as the one who pursues graduate study. The student from an affluent household will eventually manage investments, mortgages, and inheritance, while the student from a struggling household must navigate the particularly unforgiving terrain of low-margin finance, where a single overdraft fee or predatory loan can cascade into lasting harm. Renting an apartment, buying a car, choosing health insurance, understanding a pay stub, saving for emergencies, filing taxes, and evaluating the true cost of borrowing are tasks that cut across every demographic and every career path. Few other subjects in the standard curriculum can claim such universal application, and this universality is precisely what makes financial literacy a genuine life skill rather than a specialized elective.

Schools, finally, occupy a position no other institution can replicate: they reach nearly every young person during the narrow window before consequential financial decisions begin. By the time individuals encounter credit card offers in college, sign leases, take on auto loans, or commit to student debt, the opportunity for structured, equitable instruction has largely passed. Families vary enormously in their capacity to transmit financial knowledge, with many parents themselves lacking the fluency to teach what they were never taught, and this uneven inheritance perpetuates cycles of financial disadvantage along existing lines of inequality. Community programs, employer seminars, and online resources reach only those who already know to seek them out, which excludes precisely the young people most in need of guidance. Secondary schools, by contrast, encounter adolescents systematically and before the stakes rise. They are the one institution positioned to ensure that every young person, regardless of what their household can provide, enters adulthood equipped with the basic tools of financial self-governance. To decline that opportunity is to leave the most consequential domain of adult life to chance.

--- RESPONSE D ---
The transition from adolescence to adulthood is increasingly defined by complex financial decisions that young people are ill-prepared to make, leading to a pervasive cycle of economic instability. Research consistently demonstrates that the absence of formal financial education in secondary schools directly correlates with alarmingly high rates of consumer debt and financial vulnerability among young adults. Without a foundational understanding of compound interest, credit scores, and budgeting, many young people quickly accumulate high-interest credit card debt, fall prey to predatory lending practices, and struggle to manage student loans. This systemic lack of preparation leaves them highly vulnerable to economic shocks, as they often lack the knowledge required to build emergency savings or make informed decisions about basic financial products, ultimately hindering their ability to achieve long-term financial security.

Beyond mitigating financial distress, personal financial literacy is a universal life skill that offers profound benefits to every student, completely independent of their socioeconomic background or future career path. Whether a student plans to pursue a university degree, enter the trades, start a business, or transition directly into the workforce, they will inevitably have to navigate the same financial realities. Every adult must learn how to file taxes, manage a bank account, plan for retirement, and make housing decisions. By equipping all students with these essential tools, financial education democratizes economic opportunity, ensuring that individuals from lower-income backgrounds have the knowledge to build wealth and break cycles of poverty, while those from wealthier backgrounds learn to manage resources responsibly.

Furthermore, schools represent the only institution with reliable, structured access to all young people before they are forced to make high-stakes financial decisions. Relying solely on families to transmit this knowledge creates deep societal inequities, as many parents themselves may lack the training or resources to teach complex financial concepts. Secondary schools provide a standardized, objective environment where every young person can acquire these critical skills. Integrating financial literacy into the mandatory high school curriculum ensures that society proactively prepares youth before they sign their first student loan agreement, lease an apartment, or accept a credit card offer, transforming financial education from a privilege into a fundamental right.

--- RESPONSE E ---
The absence of financial education in secondary schools correlates strongly with elevated rates of consumer debt and financial vulnerability among young adults, as many enter adulthood without the tools to manage credit, budgeting, or savings effectively. This gap leaves individuals susceptible to high-interest loans, impulsive spending, and inadequate preparation for emergencies, patterns that compound over time and contribute to broader economic instability for this demographic.

Financial literacy functions as a universal life skill that delivers benefits to all students, transcending differences in family income levels or chosen career trajectories. Whether navigating entry-level wages, pursuing advanced degrees with associated costs, or handling everyday household expenses, the ability to evaluate financial options fosters greater independence and reduces the likelihood of avoidable setbacks across diverse life circumstances.

Schools stand as the only institution equipped with reliable, consistent access to all young people in the years before they confront major financial decisions such as taking on student loans, signing leases, or managing first paychecks. Mandating this subject ensures systematic exposure at an age when foundational habits can still be shaped, reaching populations that might otherwise lack structured guidance from any other source.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
